Orchot Tzadikim 9:19: And if, after a person does teshuvah, his affairs do not prosper as they did before — it is a commandment that he think in his heart that his affairs have turned to bad for his own good. For before a person did teshuvah, the Holy One, blessed be He, would pay him the reward for the commandments he performed in order to banish him from the World to Come, as it is said (Proverbs 7:10 — actually Deuteronomy 7:10), "and repays those who hate Him to their face, to destroy them." And just as He does this to those who hate Him, so He pays those who love Him the punishment for the transgressions they committed in this world, so that they be innocent and clean for the World to Come. And all this depends on the trait of joy — that one rejoice in the portion the Blessed God has allotted him.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:20: But the path by which a person rejoices in his own portion, accepting the bad with joy just as the good, divides into several paths:
Orchot Tzadikim 9:21: The first: one needs great trust in God.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:25: The wise man said: every person needs a fence, a support, and a foundation, so that his good deeds may endure. And what is the fence? This is trust — that he always trust in the Blessed God, as it is said (Psalms 55:23), "cast your burden upon the Lord, and He will sustain you."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:26: And what is the foundation of trust, and what brings a person to trust in God? This is faith! — through believing in the Creator, that all his success in this world and in the World to Come comes entirely from Him and from no one else, he gives his heart to love Him with all his heart.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:27: And what is the foundation of faith, and what brings a person to complete faith? It is that he not be shaken by any bad thing, but accept everything that comes upon him with joy. And this is like a servant who knows that his master is generous and merciful, and pays those who do his will and his errands a great reward; and even while he burdens his attendants with hard labor, he does them great good, raises them up and exalts them, makes them his counselors and lets them eat at his table, and mounts them in his own second chariot, and appoints them over his land. There is no doubt that this servant, who knows and recognizes this about his master, will abandon everything in the world and do his master's will with joy, even if the labor is very hard for him, remembering the good that will come to him because of this labor. But the servant who sees that his master withholds his servants' wages, and knows in his heart that his master is stingy, and that his toil is greater than his wage — this servant toils for his master only with grief.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:28: So it is with this matter: whoever believes with complete faith in his Maker, that He does good and shows mercy more than any who show mercy, and that He is a true Judge, and that everything He does to him is entirely for his own good, to give him great reward for everything he suffers for His great Name — and for all the service and attendance he performs for the sake of Heaven he will attain great pleasantness in the pleasant world — as we find with Nebuchadnezzar: because he took four steps in honor of the Blessed God, he merited great greatness (Sanhedrin 96a); and as we find with Esau: because he was careful about his father's honor, he merited greatness in this world, he and his offspring after him; and so with many others. There is no doubt that if a person believes all this with a whole heart, he will surely rejoice in all the judgments of the Blessed Lord, for who would not rejoice when copper coins are taken from him and a talent of gold given in their place?
Orchot Tzadikim 9:29: Whoever believes in God with a whole heart, and trusts in Him with a strong trust, this trust will bring him never to fear any bad thing, and never to serve any person other than Him in order to find favor with him, and never to hope in any man, and never to agree with them in a matter that is against the service of the Blessed Creator; and their affairs will not frighten him, and he will not be dismayed by their opposition. And if he rebukes them, he will not be careful of their honor, and if they shame him, he will not be ashamed before them, and he will not make falsehood appear pleasing for their sake, as the prophet said (Isaiah 50:7), "and the Lord God will help me, therefore I am not ashamed; therefore I have set my face like flint, and I know that I shall not be ashamed."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:30: Whoever trusts in God will be brought by this trust to free his heart from the affairs of the world, to devote himself to the matters of Torah and divine service. And a person must examine the ideas that hold his heart firm, so as to be in complete trust in God:
Orchot Tzadikim 9:31: The first thought: that he know with clear knowledge that God shows more mercy to a person than any who show mercy, and that He watches over him in secret and in the open; and at a time when he does not guard himself as he should, God shows him mercy and guards him from mishaps, as the matter is said (Psalms 116:6), "the Lord preserves the simple."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:32: The second thought: that all the good things that come to him from his father and his mother, his brothers and his relatives and his friends — all of it is from the Blessed Lord; and these are the messengers of the Blessed Omnipresent.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:33: The third: that he know that all good things come from the kindnesses of God, not that he deserves them; and the Holy One, blessed be He, does not do good to him because He needs him, but out of pure generosity and kindness.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:34: The fourth: that he know that all his affairs have a limit and an end, and no person can add to or subtract from what the exalted Creator has decreed. And what the Holy One, blessed be He, has decreed to be little for him, no person can increase, nor diminish an abundance decreed for him; and what He has decreed for another time, no person can bring forward, nor delay what He has decreed to come sooner. Rather, everything is by the decree and the will of the One above.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:35: The fifth: that he know that the Blessed Creator sees his heart, whether his trust in Him is a complete trust without deceit. For a servant who attends upon a man of flesh and blood can steal his master's heart, so that the master supposes the servant loves him with a whole heart even though he actually hates him, and the master will do him good, believing that the servant loves him. But none of this is possible with the Blessed Creator, for He knows the inclination of the heart and the thought within it, and He knows the upper and the lower realms, one's faith and one's disbelief. Therefore one cannot walk before Him with deceit.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:36: The sixth: that he take to heart to fulfill what He has commanded him, and to refrain from all that He has warned him not to do, just as he wishes that the exalted Creator do for him the thing he trusts Him for. As our Sages said (Avot 2:4): do His will as your own will, so that He may nullify the will of others before your will. But whoever trusts in the exalted Lord and does not fulfill what He commanded him — how great a fool and simpleton is he! Of this it is said (Job 27:8-9), "for what is the hope of the hypocrite, though he has gained, when God takes away his soul? Will God hear his cry when trouble comes upon him?" And it says (Jeremiah 7:9-10), "will you steal, murder, and commit adultery, and swear falsely, and burn incense to Baal, and walk after other gods whom you have not known, and then come and stand before Me in this house, which is called by My Name?!" And it says (ibid. verse 11), "is this house, which is called by My Name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?!"
Orchot Tzadikim 9:37: The seventh: that he know that the Blessed Creator created man for many kinds of work, and created his food to come through great toil and labor. And if all one's affairs, food, and clothing were prepared for a person without toil, then several commandments would become void, such as: charity, and keeping oneself far from theft, robbery, and covetousness. For if he had all his needs without toil, how would he come to crave stealing and robbing? And when he toils and yet keeps himself far from these, not coveting what is not his, then he is trusting in God. Of him the verse says (Psalms 32:10), "but he who trusts in the Lord, kindness shall surround him." And for this reason Hezekiah king of Judah hid away the Book of Remedies (Pesachim 56a), so that the sick person would trust in the exalted God, and not in remedies. Also, if a person were idle from work, and did not toil for his food, he would kick and pursue transgressions, as it is written (Deuteronomy 32:15), "and Jeshurun grew fat and kicked." And our Sages of blessed memory said (Avot 2:2): the study of Torah is pleasant together with a worldly occupation, for the toil of both makes one forget sin.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:38: But now the exalted Lord has placed two labors into man's hand: one, his own worldly work, and the second, the labor of Torah. And a person must be balanced between the two labors, and set aside dedicated hours for the labor of Torah and for worldly labor. And you must strengthen yourself to perform both labors always for your own ultimate good; and one should not undermine the other, as it is said (Jeremiah 22:15), "did not your father eat and drink, and do justice and righteousness, and then it was well with him?"; and it says (Ecclesiastes 7:18), "it is good that you take hold of the one, and also not withdraw your hand from the other." And one must trust in the Blessed Lord to make him succeed in his affairs, and not trust in his own work or affairs, but should think that his work and affairs are merely the path by which the Blessed Lord provides for him — like a man splitting wood with an axe: even though the axe cuts the wood, the power comes not from the iron, but from the man wielding the iron to cut the wood with it.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:39: And a person who has some trade or business by which he provides for his household should not think, "were it not for this trade, I would go to ruin!" Rather, he should trust in the exalted Creator, and think: if he did not have this occupation he engages in, the Blessed Creator would provide his livelihood through some other means. For all his handiwork and his needs are in the hand of God, and He has many agents, as the verse says (1 Samuel 14:6), "for there is no restraint upon the Lord to save by many or by few"; and it says (Deuteronomy 8:18), "for it is He who gives you power to get wealth"; and it says (Zechariah 4:6), "not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit, says the Lord of Hosts."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:40: And likewise a person whose whole livelihood and needs depend on one particular man should not place his trust, in his heart, upon that man, but should place the root of his trust from the depth of his heart in the Blessed Creator. And it is not enough to say this while his heart is not truly in it; rather, he should give praise and thanks to the Blessed Creator for not having withheld His kindness from him. And take to yourself a fitting parable on this matter: it is like a hundred blind men walking one behind another, each placing his hand on his fellow's shoulder, and at the head of them all is one man who can see, who leads them all after him. Behold, each of them knows that although he places his hand on his fellow's shoulder and is led by him, this guidance does not come from his fellow's own power, but that all of them are drawn along after the one seeing man at the front; and if he were removed from among them, all of them would stumble and fall. Let a person take this to heart, and think that there is no true guide but the Holy One, blessed be He, and that all of us are like blind men, each of us assisted and helped by his fellow's help; but there is no power in one's fellow were it not for the supreme Guide, who gives everything, and all of whose ways are just, and one should never suspect Him. And just as the one who is provided for should think only of the Holy One, blessed be He, so the one who provides should not become proud that he is the provider, but is rather like a blind man leading his blind fellow with the help of the first Guide, who is the one who truly sees.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:41: And of this it is said (Isaiah 42:16), "and I will lead the blind by a way they knew not, in paths they have not known I will guide them; I will make darkness light before them, and crooked things straight"; and it says (ibid. verse 18), "and the blind, look and see"; and it says (ibid. verse 19), "who is blind but My servant, or deaf as My messenger whom I send? Who is blind as he who is at peace with Me, and blind as the servant of the Lord?"
Orchot Tzadikim 9:42: And behold, all the matters in which one trusts in the Holy One, blessed be He, are eight kinds: the first, the matter of a person's own body alone; the second, the matter of his livelihood; the third, the matter of his wife; the fourth, the duties of the heart and the limbs by which he alone benefits or is harmed; the fifth, the duties of the limbs whose benefit or harm is to others; the sixth, reward in this world; the seventh, reward in the World to Come, hidden away for the righteous; the eighth, the reward of the days of the Messiah.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:43: The first trust, concerning the matter of a person's own body: that he cast his soul and give himself over to His great mercies, and know that he has no counsel or management except by His permission and His decree. And even though the entire formation of his limbs and the measure of his days are bound up in the decree of the Blessed Creator, nonetheless a person must exert himself to earn all his needs, to save his own life, and to arrange remedies for himself. And he should trust in God that He will heal him, for the physician and the remedy come to him from the Blessed Lord to heal him; and he should not leave this matter to anyone but God alone to grant him the ability and the strength. And a person should not say: since I am bound up in the decree of the exalted Creator, I will walk into paths of danger, and drink a deadly potion!
Orchot Tzadikim 9:44: Have we not found this with Samuel, when he said (1 Samuel 16:2), "how can I go? If Saul hears of it, he will kill me" — even though he said this, he was not considered as one lacking in his trust, and the Holy One, blessed be He, answered him: "take a heifer with you" (ibid.).
Orchot Tzadikim 9:45: And of whoever puts himself in danger and says, "I am trusting in the Blessed Lord!" it is said (Proverbs 14:16), "but the fool is arrogant and confident." And the Torah warned us of this, as it is written (Deuteronomy 6:16), "you shall not test the Lord your God." And whoever puts himself in danger and causes his own death — his punishment is greater than that of one who kills others.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:46: The second trust, concerning the matter of livelihood: his trust should be upon the Blessed Lord, that He will provide his needs and his food sufficient for him, and he should not press the moment to pursue many affairs that distract him from occupying himself with Torah. And when he trusts in God, he will find rest for his heart and ease for his soul, and will not pursue [wealth] excessively; rather, it will be enough for him to obtain what he can in a set time, and in the remaining hours he shall labor to acquire the life of the World to Come.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:47: And so they said (Sifrei, Va'etchanan 6:7): increase your sitting [in study] and decrease your business dealings; make the words of Torah your main concern and your business dealings secondary. And this matter is the greatest of a person's trials — that the great preoccupations of this world not distract him so that he forgets his ultimate end. Therefore he should trust in God that He will provide his needs and his sufficiency, so that he may have free hours to devote his heart to God.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:48: The third trust, concerning the matter of his wife, children, relatives, and friends: if this trusting person is a stranger, dwelling without a wife, relatives, or friends, let him take God as his relative and his friend, as it is written (Song of Songs 5:16), "this is my beloved, and this is my friend." And let him think: whoever has relatives will, after a short time, return to a strange grave and sit alone, and neither relative, nor son, nor friend will help him, and not one of them will accompany him there. And let him then think about the burden of relatives placed upon him, and consider this for the good: that if he were occupied with the affairs of this world, his toil would be great and he would have no rest; but if he is occupied with the matters of God's unity and the commandments, and the devotion of his heart to God, his heart will be freer and more devoted at a time he is alone without his relatives — there is no doubt of this. And for this reason the ascetics who devoted their hearts to God alone would flee their homes and their relatives for the mountains, so as to devote their hearts to God.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:49: And if this trusting person has a wife, children, relatives, and friends, let him trust in God to give him the strength to pay them what he owes them and to fulfill their wishes, and let him trust that his heart will be with them, and that he will teach them the paths of Torah and the service of the Creator — not because he expects to gain some benefit from them because of this, nor that they will honor him for showing them the upright path, nor to dominate them; rather, he should do it solely to fulfill the commandment of the Blessed Creator. And he should think that he is an agent of the Omnipresent to teach his relatives and his friends, and should not credit himself for it, nor let his heart be haughty toward them. And if he should need something from his relatives, and they fill his want, let him think that they are agents of the Blessed Omnipresent to fill his want, and not trust in them at all. And if he asks something of them and they turn him away empty-handed, let him not hold it against them as a sin, but think that the Omnipresent has many agents to fill his want.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:50: The fourth trust, concerning the duty of the heart: that a person devote his heart to fasting, prayer, and all the other commandments, and refrain from transgressions. And he must go with all his strength to fulfill the commandments, and pray with a faithful heart and a clean mind, with intent directed to His great Name. And in this we are obligated to trust in Him and to supplicate Him, to help us and to show us the straight paths, as David, peace upon him, said (Psalms 25:5), "lead me in Your truth and teach me"; and it says (ibid. 119:35), "lead me in the path of Your commandments"; and it says (ibid. verse 30), "I have chosen the way of faith." And all this is proof that he chose the practice of divine service. And he should pray about two things: first, to strengthen his heart in devotion to God, and that he keep the preoccupation of this world far from his heart; and second, to strengthen him in his body and his limbs, so that he be able to strengthen himself in good deeds. And this is what he said, that He should give him success in his body and in the devotion of his heart to God.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:51: The fifth trust is the duty of the limbs by which one occupies himself in doing good to others — such as charity, teaching wisdom to students, commanding what is good and keeping far from evil, bringing the wicked back to God, and bearing their disgrace when he warns them about divine service and threatens them with reward and punishment. And he should toil with all his strength to do these things, and trust in God that He will help him; and he should fulfill his desire in this only to draw close to God, and not to gain a reputation or honor among people because of it, nor to expect reward from them, nor to dominate them. And he should take care, as much as he is able, to keep this hidden; and if he cannot keep it hidden, let him remember that all benefit and harm come not from created beings but only by permission of the Blessed Creator. And in all of this he should place his trust in the Blessed Lord. And when the exalted Lord causes a commandment to come about through him, let him think in his heart that this is a good thing from the exalted Creator, who has done good to him, and let him not rejoice if people praise him for it.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:52: The sixth trust, concerning this world: that he trust in God that He will not make him consume, in this world, the portion due to him in the World to Come. And let him trust in Him that He will guard him from the mishaps of the world, from illnesses, from pestilence and sword and famine, and from the other evils that arise to come into the world.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:53: And when he trusts, let him not trust because of his own good deeds; rather, let him do all his deeds for the sake of the exalted God, who raised him up and exalted him in this world and did good to him, and there is not a single moment of all his days in which the good things of the Creator are not upon him. And let him think that even if his deeds were multiplied many times over, they would not amount to one part in ten thousand of what he is obligated to do because of the goodness of the Blessed God, which is upon him at every moment. And after he considers all this, let him trust in the kindnesses of the Blessed Lord, who does kindness and shows more mercy than any deed of man, for in His mercy He gives bread to the creeping things and to the beasts and to the wild animals and to the birds, and He sustains from the horns of wild oxen to the eggs of lice (Avodah Zarah 3b); and just as He shows mercy to these not because of their good deeds, so may He show mercy to me.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:54: The seventh trust: that he trust in the King of kings who rules over all, blessed be He, that in his days He will bring salvation to Israel, and build Jerusalem, and build the Temple in his days. And the intent of his trust should not be in order to live in great ease as will be in those days, and to eat fine fruits and drink sweet wine; rather, the intent of his trust should be that he live in those days in order to serve the Blessed Creator — for in those days He will remove the evil inclination from the heart of His people, and all of them, small and great, will know the Lord. And nothing will hinder them: neither pestilence nor famine, neither war nor preoccupation; rather, all of them will be free, and all of them will attain a great grasp of the knowledge of the Blessed Creator. And in those days knowledge will increase, as it is written (Isaiah 11:9), "for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea."
Orchot Tzadikim 9:55: The eighth trust, concerning the matter of the World to Come: in which there is pleasantness without end and without limit, and no mouth can describe the beauty of that world, and no eye can see the splendor of the glory of the righteous. And there is no eating or drinking there — if so, what pleasure is there there? For this you must understand and know: just as a bird does not know the pleasure of a fish swimming in the water, because their natures are opposite one another — a bird will die in water and a fish will die on dry land — so one who is in this world, whose soul is intermingled with the body, cannot know the pleasure of souls; for we know only bodily pleasure, but the pleasure of the supernal delights we cannot attain, nor can we recognize them except after much reflection. And this is because we are in a world of bodies, and therefore we recognize only pleasures that perish and cease. But the pleasures of the soul are forever without end, and there is no connection or partnership, nor any closeness in any matter, between those pleasures and these. And whoever merits that level after his death will not love these [bodily] pleasures, just as a king would not love to strip off his glorious splendor and play in the streets with children. And it sometimes happens that a king, being young in years, lets the folly of children overpower him, and plays with the young, forsaking the glory of his kingship — and this is because he lacks the understanding to discern between the two paths, just as we let the pleasure of this world overpower the pleasure of the World to Come because of the deficiency of our understanding and our meager awareness of the world of souls and its delights.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:56: And in this world you can recognize a little of the world of souls, from the pleasures of the soul that come without eating or drinking: such as people who take revenge on their enemies, and such as honor, at the time people honor a person, and when a person sees beautiful things, or when a person sees his beloved son whom he has not seen for a long time, or when he hears good tidings. In all of these there is great pleasure without eating or drinking, and if this happens in the world of bodies, where we see that souls derive enjoyment — from this you can understand the pleasure of souls when the soul ascends to the heavens above, and enjoys the splendor of the supernal world and the splendor of the Divine Presence.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:57: And that pleasure has no description and no depiction, and we cannot compare it to any pleasure in this world; rather, as the prophet said, being astonished and amazed at the glory of the World to Come (Psalms 31:20), "how great is Your goodness, which You have hidden away for those who fear You." And concerning the World to Come, which is the ultimate end of every person, let him place his trust in the Lord that He bring him to the supernal world, and let him not cast this trust away from before him.
Orchot Tzadikim 9:58: And he has no [true] trust without good deeds; rather, after he occupies himself with all his ability in Torah and good deeds, he will rise to the levels of piety fitting for this matter. And this is that he remove the love of this world from his heart, and put in its place love of the Blessed Creator, and give himself over for the sanctification of the Blessed Name.
